newsitem.title: USA: U.S. labor mkts tight, no slackening - Fed sources.
newsitem.headline: U.S. labor mkts tight, no slackening - Fed sources.

text.p: U.S. labor markets remain tight and there seems to be very little on the economic horizon to suggest the unemployment rate is likely to rise much further than its current 5.0 percent level, Federal Reserve sources said.

"There is no evidence of a slackening labor market. In fact, the evidence seems to gradually be mounting in the other direction. The need for workers persists," a source at the Federal Reserve, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.
"The pool of qualified workers apparently is not expanding ... indicating that perhaps we may see a continued tightening (of labor markets)," the source added.
A second source at the Federal Reserve, who also asked not to be named, agreed, adding that companies still seem to be having a hard time finding workers.
Some of those firms, the source added, are said to be turning down some orders because they have not been able to keep up with demand. "Labor markets are still tight," the second source said.

Comments on the continued tighteness of labor markets gain particular relevance after official figures released last week showed the country's jobless rate rose to 5.0 percent in June from 4.8 percent the previous month.

The small rise in the unemployment rate, coupled with a slowdown in job growth in the private sector, sparked a strong rally on Wall Street, pushing stock and bond prices up while long-term interest rates fell.

"One imagines that the job growth numbers suggest that we might continue to see that sort of impact on the unemployment rate: month to month bounces around, not much standing," the first Fed source said.
Fed sources said, however, wage pressures have remained scattered, indicating that inflationary pressures are not a major threat for now.
"We do see some wage pressures here and there, but the fact is that they haven't really been filtering down to retail prices as of yet," the second Fed source said.
Fed sources said the phenomenon could be the result of increased productivity in the economy.

"While some firms recognize that there are some -- albeit modest -- cost pressures, they also often tell us that their profit margins aren't shrinking because of increased productivity," the first Fed source said.
But the source was still skeptical about the notion that higher productivity and increased global competition could put a permanent lid on inflation.
"But then, when you ask whether inflation is dead as a result (of increased productivity) the answer there apparently is that it is not," the Fed source said.
The source acknowledged the current economic scenario has brought some changes to the way economists look at inflation.
But the source added that classic economic concepts still apply and inflation is not dead because productivity might be on the rise and global competition stiffer.
"If that increase in productivity is trend productivity, if it's long lasting, it will show itself in higher real interest rates.
"If that is the case, then interest rates at any point in time could perhaps not reflect a balance, and it might allow for some inflationary pressures," the source said.
